tier_reason: A peer-reviewed paper (Muła & Lemire, ACM TWEB, doi 10.1145/3132709, arXiv 1704.00605) names this repo as its software. The paper benchmarks the codec against Chrome's codec (src/chromiumbase64.c) using benchmarks/basic_benchmark.c, and it states GNU GCC 5.3, -O3 -march=native and an Intel i7-6700, so every tier A condition is met. The cited Turbo-Base64 page on its own would support only C, because its comparison harness is not public and it gives no flags.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Paper (i7-6700, GCC 5.3 -O3 -march=native): for large random inputs the AVX2 codec uses about 0.25 cycles per input byte, against Chrome's codec at about 2.7 (encode) and 1.8 (decode). The paper calls this 'eleven times faster at encoding and over seven times faster at decoding'. In Table VI, decoding real files takes 0.21-0.27 cycles/byte against Chrome's 1.8-2.1 (lena: 0.21 vs 1.8). In an independent table in the Turbo-Base64 README (i7-9700K, gcc 11.2, 1 MB), fb64avx2 runs at 23,686/21,231 MB/s encode/decode against Google Chrome base64 at 2,541/4,289 MB/s (about 9.3x encode and 4.9x decode, derived from page data).
corrections.workload: Single-threaded base64 decoding of real base64 payloads: the lena, peppers and mandril JPEGs, a Moby Dick quote, and Google and Bing inline images. Encoding and decoding of random data of varying size. Measured in cycles per input byte with rdtsc, Turbo Boost disabled, minimum of 500 runs. Secondary: 1 MB encode/decode in the Turbo-Base64 README table.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: GNU GCC 5.3, -O3 -march=native (paper; the repo Makefile also sets -O3 -march=native -mavx2). Turbo-Base64 table: gcc 11.2, no flags stated.
corrections.hardware: Intel Core i7-6700 (Skylake) @ 3.4 GHz, Turbo Boost disabled, 32 GB DDR4-2133 (paper); Intel i7-9700K @ 3.6 GHz (Turbo-Base64 table)
corrections.caveats: The paper's numbers date from 2017. The repo is archived, and its README says it is unmaintained research code, not for production, and that users should switch to simdutf. The AVX2 codec needs AVX2 hardware and falls back to scalar code for short inputs (under about 100 bytes it gains nothing). Turbo-Base64's source comments call fastbase64 'unsafe, can reads/writes beyound i/o buffers'; that is a competitor's claim and is unverified.

notes: I moved the evidence to the peer-reviewed paper, whose artifact is this repo. The Turbo-Base64 numbers in the original claim are accurate and belong to the fb64avx2 row, but that harness is closed and gives no flags. The paper and algorithm are the same as in the WojciechMula/base64simd record in this batch, and the successor is simdutf, so dedupe with care. GitHub reports the license as NOASSERTION, but the LICENSE file is the standard BSD 2-clause text.

tier_reason: A peer-reviewed paper (ACM TWEB, arXiv 1704.00605) shows the Muła/Lemire AVX2 algorithms beating Chrome's codec by about 11x on encode and 7x on decode, with GCC 5.3 -O3 -march=native on an i7-6700 stated. However, the paper's public benchmark harness and the codec it measured live in lemire/fastbase64 (benchmarks/basic_benchmark.c), not in this repo. base64simd's own benchmark programs and results (decode/results/*.csv, encode/results/*.txt, benchmark_results/) compare only against its own scalar routines. That makes it B, not A.

corrections.hardware: Intel Core i7-6700 (Skylake) @ 3.4 GHz, Turbo Boost disabled, 32 kB L1d / 256 kB L2 / 8 MB L3 (paper Section 5)
corrections.claimed_speedup: Paper: for large random inputs the AVX2 codec uses about 0.25 cycles per input byte, against Chrome's codec at about 2.7 (encode) and 1.8 (decode). The paper calls this 'eleven times faster at encoding and over seven times faster at decoding'; the abstract rounds to about 10x and 7x. In Table VI, decoding real files takes 0.21-0.27 cycles/byte against Chrome's 1.8-2.1. The repo README, comparing against its own scalar code only, reports 2-4x faster encoding and 2-2.7x faster decoding.
corrections.caveats: The paper's measured codec and its benchmark harness are in lemire/fastbase64; this repo is Muła's research harness of algorithm variants (SSE, AVX2, AVX-512, BMI2, NEON, XOP), each benchmarked only against its own scalar versions. Its README says the code does not process the data tail or '=' padding, so it is not a spec-complete codec; it points users to aklomp/base64 and lemire/fastbase64 for that. The paper, the algorithm and the Chrome comparison are the same as in the lemire/fastbase64 record.

notes: The numbers are quoted correctly from the paper, but they measure fastbase64's implementation, not this repo's code, so I set the tier to B. Consider merging this entry with lemire/fastbase64, or keeping it as the algorithm-origin entry. The metadata checks out: BSD-2-Clause, 172 stars, not a fork, last commit 2025-02-21 (stale). I did not verify the simdutf/Node/Chromium usage claim.

tier_reason: The README's i7-9700K tables (gcc 11.2) compare against Google Chrome and Linux base64 and against the aklomp and fastbase64 AVX2 codecs. The numbers are first-party, though, and the harness that links those competitor codecs is not in the public repo. tb64app.c only #includes xb64test.h and xtb64test_.c under XBASE64, and the makefile includes xtb64.mak; none of those files are in the tree or the 2023.04/2023.08 tags. The page also states no flags, so this is first-party with partial methodology: C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: On the i7-9700K with gcc 11.2 and a 1 MB buffer (2022.02), tb64v256 AVX2 runs at 29,086/29,748 MB/s encode/decode. That compares with Google Chrome base64 at 2,541/4,289 MB/s (about 11.4x encode and 6.9x decode, derived from page data), lemire fb64avx2 at 23,686/21,231 and aklomp b64avx2 at 26,153/22,515. At 50,000 B, tb64v256 reaches 32,794/37,837 MB/s against b64avx2 at 27,789/22,264 and fb64avx2 at 25,305/21,980. On the Ryzen 9 7950X (gcc 12.2, 1 MB, 2023.07), tb64v512vbmi reaches 77,619/76,716 MB/s, but it is compared only with its own variants and with memcpy (37,047/31,694), with no external baseline on that machine.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: gcc-12.2 (Ryzen 9 7950X, 2023.07); gcc 11.2 (i7-9700K, 2022.02). The README states no flags. The public makefile uses -O3 with -march=haswell for the AVX2 file and -march=skylake-avx512 -mavx512vbmi for the AVX-512 file.
corrections.workload: Single-thread encode/decode with error checking. On the AMD Ryzen 9 7950X: 1,000,000 B and 10,000 B buffers. On the Intel i7-9700K: 50,000 B, 1 MB and short strings of 4-128 B. There are also ARM tables (Apple M1, ODROID-N2).
corrections.caveats: The numbers are first-party. The build that includes competitor codecs (XBASE64=1: xtb64.mak, xb64test.h, xtb64test_.c) is not public, so the cross-library tables cannot be reproduced from the repo. The Ryzen 7950X AVX-512 table has no Chrome or other external row. The original claim divided 7950X numbers by the i7-9700K Chrome row, a cross-machine ratio, and '~10-18x' was also miscomputed. The README benchmark tables were last updated in August 2023. The code is GPL-3.0 with a commercial license available.

notes: The claimed ratio was invalid because it mixed machines; I replaced it with same-table i7-9700K ratios. The metadata checks out: GPL-3.0, 340 stars, not a fork, not archived, last commit 2026-06-28 (active). I found no independent benchmark: Algolia search of HN turned up only the author's own Show HN posts, and the Muła/Lemire AVX-512 paper (arXiv 1910.05109) does not test it.
